insight.title: AI moves from pilots to the operating model
insight.body: For an energy major, the near-term value of enterprise AI concentrates in four functions: trading analytics, predictive maintenance, safety assurance and back-office automation. The decision in front of the business is no longer whether to adopt but which platform combination to standardise on, under which governance regime, and with which delivery partner. The tabs in this view walk that decision end to end: exposure, talent, trust and the weighted assessment.

kpis.label: AI OPPORTUNITY
kpis.definition: 0 to 100, higher is stronger. Where AI helps the functions of the business.
kpis.tooltip: Composite of function-level opportunity signals across the organisation.

kpis.label: AI THREAT EXPOSURE
kpis.definition: 0 to 100, higher means more disruption risk to current ways of working.

kpis.definition: 0 to 100, higher is more ready. AI skills density and training reach.

kpis.label: GOVERNANCE POSTURE
kpis.definition: 0 to 100, higher is stronger. Controls and compliance readiness for AI deployment.

questions: Which of our functions gain most from agentic AI this year?
What does the EU AI Act require of our safety-critical use cases?
Which vendor shortlist fits our governance posture?
Who should deliver our AI programme, and at what readiness?

aiExposure.summary: AI helps more than it threatens across the portfolio: trading, maintenance and safety functions carry high evidenced opportunity, while clerical and document-heavy functions face the largest workflow disruption. Readiness is mid-pack for the sector and improving.

functionExposure.note: Signal extraction, scenario generation and hedging analytics with human sign-off.
Asset telemetry models cut unplanned downtime; well-evidenced sector pattern.
Anomaly detection and permit-to-work document checking; regulator-sensitive.
Highest workflow disruption: document processing and reconciliation.

keyFindings: Opportunity concentrates in functions with rich telemetry and document flows
Threat exposure is highest where work is clerical and rules-based
Sector peers are standardising on two-platform strategies with one frontier and one incumbent stack
Delivery capability, not model quality, is the binding constraint this year
recommendations: Prioritise maintenance and trading use cases with measurable baselines
Stand up a model-agnostic orchestration layer before deepening any single vendor dependency
Route safety-critical use cases through the strictest applicable regime (EU AI Act high-risk) by default
Contract delivery partners against the AI readiness ranking, not headline day rates

talent.insight: The workforce skews technical for the sector, with strong engineering depth but a thin dedicated AI specialist bench relative to ambition. Training reach is widening; the constraint is experienced applied-AI leadership in the functions.
talent.pyramidMetric: AI literacy index by level, 0 to 100

leadership.speaker: Group technology leadership
leadership.quote: Sample signal: public statements emphasise scaling AI in maintenance and trading with human accountability retained.

leadership.speaker: Trading leadership
leadership.quote: Sample signal: analytics investment framed as decision support, not autonomous execution.

aiTalentExposure.summary: Just under half the workforce sits in roles where AI changes a material share of tasks. Growth concentrates in applied AI engineering, data product and AI assurance roles.

governance.summary: Governance posture is strong for the sector: an established risk framework extends naturally to AI assurance, and board oversight of digital risk is in place. The gap to close is AI-specific: model inventories, deployment gates and documentation that satisfies the EU AI Act's high-risk requirements where they apply.
keyFindings: Enterprise risk framework adapts well to AI assurance duties
Model inventory and use-case registry are partial, not complete
Supplier AI clauses lag the pace of procurement
Safety-critical deployments will attract high-risk classification in the EU
recommendations: Complete the AI use-case registry before the next audit cycle
Gate high-risk deployments behind documented conformity checks
Standardise AI clauses in vendor and integrator contracts
Assign named accountability for each production model

regulatoryGrid.note: General-purpose AI obligations apply from August 2025; high-risk system requirements phase in through 2026 and 2027. Safety-critical industrial use cases likely qualify as high-risk.
No horizontal statute; sector regulators apply five cross-cutting principles. Financial trading AI falls under existing conduct rules.
No comprehensive federal statute; export controls on advanced chips shape infrastructure choices. Sector agencies police claims and safety.
Transparency and safety-disclosure obligations for large model developers affect vendor selection more than deployment.
Duties on deployers of high-risk AI systems in consequential decisions; relevant to HR and customer-facing uses.
Government-use focused with narrower private-sector duties; monitor for energy-sector guidance.
Bias audit duties for automated hiring tools; applies to talent workflows.

regulatoryGrid.regime: EU AI Act plus national supervision
regulatoryGrid.note: National market surveillance authorities enforce; works councils add co-determination duties for workplace AI.

regulatoryGrid.regime: EU AI Act plus CNIL guidance
regulatoryGrid.note: Data protection authority active on AI and personal data; relevant to customer analytics.
No horizontal AI statute; data protection law and sector advisories govern. Large delivery-centre exposure makes workforce transition rules the watch item.

vendorRulings.note: Documentation and transparency duties sit with model providers; deployers inherit downstream duties. Confidence-labelled from the AIE legislation material.
Shapes where sovereign and regional AI capacity can be built; a supply-chain consideration for global deployment. Seeded from the AIE market signals dataset.

dimensions.label: Strategic fit
dimensions.rationale: The highest-value use cases (trading, maintenance, safety) align with proven sector patterns and existing data assets.

subcriteria.label: Use-case value concentration
subcriteria.note: Four functions carry most of the value.

dimensions.label: Execution readiness
dimensions.rationale: Engineering depth is real but the applied-AI bench is thin; delivery partners will carry early scale.

subcriteria.label: Internal capability
subcriteria.note: Specialist bench small relative to ambition.

subcriteria.label: Delivery channel strength
subcriteria.note: Strong integrator options; see live readiness ranking.

dimensions.label: Governance and trust
dimensions.rationale: Strong enterprise risk machinery; AI-specific controls partially built. EU high-risk duties are the pacing item.

subcriteria.label: Regulatory exposure
subcriteria.note: High-risk classification likely for safety-critical uses.

subcriteria.label: Vendor trust posture
subcriteria.note: Shortlist must clear governance bar; see Trust Rank.

dimensions.label: Economics
dimensions.rationale: Falling inference prices and credible multi-vendor leverage favour committing now with staged spend.

subcriteria.label: Value evidence
subcriteria.note: Baselines exist for maintenance; thinner elsewhere.

subcriteria.label: Lock-in risk
subcriteria.note: Manageable at the application layer if orchestration stays model-agnostic.

derivation.method: Weighted sum of four dimension scores, each 0 to 100. Dimension scores are the evidence-weighted mean of their subcriteria. Weights reflect a buyer decision where strategic fit dominates.
derivation.formula: weightedTotal = sum(weight_i x score_i), weights sum to 1.0
derivation.confidenceNote: All values SAMPLE for the exemplar buyer. In production each subcriterion cites its evidence items and claims below the strong-evidence bar are suppressed.
derivation.schemaNote: Shape mirrors GET /assessment/framework (dimensions, weights, rationales, subcriteria) so a live buyer assessment is a data swap.
